title: A Well for the Cellar
premise: Emrys Crane, a property surveyor who has spent a decade rationalizing the noises in his rented cellar, takes on the appraisal of Hollowmere House and discovers its walls respond to measurement, whispering back figures he never spoke. As the harvest moon approaches, he learns the house is bound to a drowned girl whose family sang a four-verse song to keep her sleeping, and that his own sleep recordings contain a second voice answering questions in his cadence. To survive, Emrys must learn the song's final verse without singing along, while confronting that the voice is the self he buried when he chose duty over love years ago. In the end he sings the verse silently, offering the house his hidden self as a substitute, freeing the girl and walking out hollow but honest, the appraisal complete at a price no ledger can hold.
about_author: Coral Pemberton is the pen name of a former rural surveyor who spent years cataloguing houses that refused to stay empty. They write horror from the conviction that every building remembers who tried to disappear inside it.

chapters.title: The Square Footage of Silence
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Emrys, who arrives at Hollowmere House to appraise it for a probate sale and finds the tape measure pulling taut on its own. He catalogs creaks, drafts, settling beams. Emotional beat: brittle professionalism stretched over a decade of practiced denial.

chapters.title: Inventory of Small Noises
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. He sets up his sleep recorder out of habit, telling himself it's for the report. The cellar door, which he never opens, is warm to the touch. A neighbor mentions the previous owner left 'everything below stairs' in the sale. Beat: the first crack in rationalization.

chapters.title: What the Walls Answer
chapters.summary: Emrys calls out measurements aloud as surveyors do, and the house echoes them back with corrections, always lower, always truer. He documents it as acoustic anomaly. Beat: fascination curdling into the thrill of being noticed after years of invisibility.

chapters.title: The Recording, First Playback
chapters.summary: Emrys reviews the night's audio: his own sleep-talk, then a second voice, softer, answering questions he doesn't remember asking. The voice knows his mother's nickname for him. Beat: vertigo, the sense that his privacy was never private.

chapters.title: Miss Aldous of the Parish Records
chapters.summary: Emrys visits the village archivist, Edith Aldous, who recognizes the house's name and goes pale. She gives him a partial history: the Verrow family, 1893, a daughter lost to the well behind the kitchen. Beat: dread acquiring a shape and a date.

chapters.title: Four Verses, Three Surviving
chapters.summary: Third-person on Emrys in the archive. Edith shows him a hymnal with a lullaby transcribed in a child's hand, the fourth verse torn out. She warns him: the house sings it back if you let it finish for you. Beat: the rules of the game revealed.

chapters.title: Questions in My Own Voice
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, night. The second voice begins asking questions: what did you bury, who did you leave, why do you measure things instead of touching them. He answers before he can stop himself. Beat: the horror of self-recognition.

chapters.title: The Man He Was Before
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Emrys's POV. Ten years ago he abandoned a partner, Tomas, choosing his father's surveying firm and respectability over a life that would have made him visible. Beat: grief and shame surfacing, the theme of love against duty made explicit.

chapters.title: The Well Behind the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Emrys finds the capped well, its stone cover scored with fingernail grooves from inside. The house hums the first verse as he stands there, and he catches himself humming along. Beat: terror at his own complicity.

chapters.title: Edith's Refusal
chapters.summary: Third-person. Emrys begs Edith for the missing verse; she refuses, saying the last woman who sang it whole was found in the cellar with her mouth full of well water. Beat: the cost of knowledge made concrete; isolation deepens.

chapters.title: The Appraisal That Appraises
chapters.summary: Emrys attempts to finish his professional report; the house rewrites his figures, valuing the property in years of a life rather than currency. The final line reads: 'One occupant, unaccounted for.' Beat: duty and the supernatural converge; he cannot do his job without engaging the haunting.

chapters.title: A Second Set of Footprints
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Wet footprints, child-sized, appear from the cellar to his bed. The voice in the recordings is now singing the first three verses flawlessly, waiting. Beat: the deadline, the harvest moon, becomes tangible.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Stayed Invisible
chapters.summary: Emrys seeks out the previous tenant, Ruth Callow, living in a caravan outside town, who never sang, never answered, and left when the moon rose. She tells him invisibility is a payment the house accepts, but only once. Beat: false hope offered and poisoned.

chapters.title: The Voice Has His Face
chapters.summary: Third-person. In a dream, Emrys meets the second voice wearing his own younger face, the self from before Tomas, before the firm. It offers to sing the verse for him if he'll only stay. Beat: temptation, the seduction of surrender.

chapters.title: Tomas on the Telephone
chapters.summary: Emrys, desperate, calls Tomas after ten years. The conversation is awkward, tender, unfinished. Tomas says: 'You always measured everything so you'd never have to hold anything.' Beat: love re-entering as both wound and possible salvation.

chapters.title: The Verse in the Well Water
chapters.summary: Emrys lowers a recorder on a string into the well; the playback returns the fourth verse, sung by a drowned girl's voice, addressed to whoever is brave enough to learn it. Beat: awe and pity; the monster reframed as a wronged child awaiting justice.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession
chapters.summary: Edith admits her grandmother was the Verrow maid who let the girl drown rather than reveal her own theft, then tore out the verse to keep the house bound and quiet. Beat: justice outside the law; the true crime surfaces, and Edith begs Emrys to finish what her family began.

chapters.title: Rehearsal Without Voice
chapters.summary: Emrys memorizes the fourth verse silently, mouthing it, refusing to let air carry it. The house retaliates: doors vanish, the cellar door appears in every room. Beat: rising tension; the rules tighten as the moon fattens.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The moon rises full and orange over Hollowmere. The house sings all four verses at once, the fourth in his own buried voice, and every part of him wants to join. Beat: the climax's threshold, will at its breaking point.

chapters.title: The Song's Last Verse
chapters.summary: Climax, third-person. In the cellar, Emrys mouths the final verse without sound, then speaks the truth of his buried self aloud instead of singing, offering his hidden years as the payment. The well exhales; the drowned girl, unbound, forgives him by simply leaving. Beat: sacrifice of the false self.

chapters.title: Appraised at Nothing
chapters.summary: Emrys files his report valuing Hollowmere at zero, unsellable, and recommends it stand empty as a memorial. Edith adds her family's confession to the parish record. Beat: justice rendered outside any court; quiet catharsis.

chapters.title: The Verse He Keeps
chapters.summary: Resolution, Emrys's POV. He visits Tomas with the recording of the fourth verse and, for the first time, sings along, voice cracking, visible at last. The final line: some songs are only safe once you stop singing them alone. Beat: love chosen over duty; the self made whole.
